title: De Natura et Gratia
author: Augustine
source: Translated by Claude from stoa0040.stoa054.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's CSEL.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.
availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit Open Greek and Latin's CSEL and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

passages.original: Beatus uero Hilarius, cuius haec uerba posuit: non enim nisi spiritu per fecti et inmortalitate mutati, quod solis mundis corde d e d i dispositum est, hoc quod in deo est inmortale cernemus, quod dixit contra id quod dicimus uel quid istum adiuuet nescio, nisi quia posse esse hominem mundo corde testatus est. quod quis negat? sed gratia dei per Iesum Christum.
passages.english: As for blessed Hilary, whose words he has quoted, "For only when we have been made perfect in spirit and changed by immortality, which has been appointed for the pure in heart alone, shall we see that which is immortal in God": I do not know what he said against what we say, or what in it helps this man, except that he testified that a man can be pure in heart. Who denies that? But [it is] by the grace of God through Jesus Christ
passages.notes: "d e d i" is read as a scanning error, probably for "a deo" ("appointed by God"); it is left untranslated. The sentence continues into the following context ("our Lord, not by freedom of choice alone").

passages.original: ecce quid iste sapiat, si uerbis Ambrosii delectatur, quod a deo praeparatur uoluntas hominum, et nulla uel non magna quaestio est, quis uel quando perficiatur, dum tamen sine Christi gratia id ipsum fieri posse minime dubitetur. deinde quantum erat, ut adtenderet iste unum uersum de Ambrosii uerbis quae posuit! cum enim ille dixisset : nam cum ecclesia ex gentibus, hoc est ex peccatoribus, congregata sit, quomodo e x maculatis inmaculata potest esse, nisi primo per Christi gratiam abluta delicto sit, deinde quod per qualitatem non peccandi abstineat a delictis ? ille addidit, quod iste apparet cur addere noluerit, ait namque ille: nec ab initio inmaculata-humanae enim hoc inpossibile naturae —, sed per dei gratiam et qualitatem sui, quia iam non peccat, fit ut inmaculata uideatur.
passages.english: See what this man would understand, if he takes pleasure in the words of Ambrose: that the will of men is prepared by God, and that it is no question, or no great one, who is made perfect or when, provided only that there is no doubt at all that this very thing cannot happen without the grace of Christ. Then, how much it would have taken for him to attend to a single line of the words of Ambrose that he quoted! For when Ambrose had said, "For since the Church has been gathered from the gentiles, that is, from sinners, how can it be immaculate [when it comes] from the stained, unless it has first been washed from wrongdoing by the grace of Christ, and then, by the quality of not sinning, abstains from wrongdoing?", he added something that this man evidently did not want to add [himself], and it is plain why. For Ambrose says: "Nor [was it] immaculate from the beginning, for this is impossible for human nature; but through the grace of God and its own quality, because it no longer sins, it comes about that it appears immaculate."
passages.notes: "minime dubitetur" is taken in the sense the argument needs: there is no doubt that this cannot happen without Christ's grace. Read literally, the Latin says "that it can happen", which looks like a slip in the text. "Qualitas" is kept as "quality"; it means the condition or character of not sinning.

passages.original: librum ergo, quo huic respondi defendens gratiam non contra naturam, sed per quam natura liberatur et regitur, De natura et gratia nuncupaui. in quo uerba quaedam, quae uelut Xysti Romani episcopi et martyris Pelagius posuit, ita defendi, tamquam re uerba eiusdem Xysti essent — id enim putaueram —, sed postea legi Sexti philosophi esse, non Xysti Christiani.
passages.english: So the book in which I answered him, defending grace not as opposed to nature but as that through which nature is set free and governed, I named On Nature and Grace. In it I defended certain words which Pelagius had put forward as being those of Xystus, bishop of Rome and martyr, as though they really were the words of that same Xystus (for that is what I had supposed); but afterwards I read that they belonged to Sextus the philosopher, not to Xystus the Christian.
passages.notes: "re uerba" is read as "re uera" ("really"), an evident scanning or printing error.
